Thine
thīn
pronominal adj. and pron. (second person singular possessive; rendering Hebrew suffix -ka, Greek sos and sou)
From Saxon þin, the uncontracted possessive of þu. It serves two offices: before a vowel or h it does the work of thy (thine heart, thine eyes), and standing alone it is the absolute possessive (the kingdom is thine).

Biblical Definition

Thine is the fuller form of thy, and the Authorized Version employs it in two distinct ways. Before a word beginning with a vowel or with h it simply replaces thy for the sake of the ear: “with all thine heart”, “open, LORD, thine eyes”, “the work of thine hands”. Standing by itself, without a noun following, it is the absolute possessive — the form in which a worshipper renders everything back to God. Hezekiah spreads the Assyrian letter before the LORD and prays, “bow down thine ear, and hear: open, LORD, thine eyes, and see” (2 Kings 19:16), asking God to turn His own faculties toward a threat too large for Judah. Micah promises the LORD will destroy what Israel has made: “thou shalt no more worship the work of thine hands” (Micah 5:13) — the possessive convicting, because the idol belongs to the man who carved it. And Melchizedek blesses Abram by naming the enemies as God's business: “which hath delivered thine enemies into thy hand” (Genesis 14:20). The word is small and the doctrine large: what is thine is what will be answered for.

Webster 1828 Definition

The possessive of thou, used before a vowel or h in place of thy, and used absolutely without a following noun. In Scripture it appears in the great phrases of devotion — thine heart, thine eyes, the work of thine hands.

expand to see more

THINE, pronom. adj. [Sax. þin.] Thy; belonging to thee; the possessive of thou.

2. It is used before a word beginning with a vowel or with h, where thy would be harsh; as thine heart, thine eyes.

3. It is also used without a noun following, as the absolute possessive; as, the kingdom is thine.

4. In the older writers it stands where modern usage would require thy in every place.

5. In Scripture, bow down thine ear, and hear, 2 Kings 19; the work of thine hands, Micah 5.

Key Scripture

2 Kings 19:16 — "LORD, bow down thine ear, and hear: open, LORD, thine eyes, and see: and hear the words of Sennacherib, which hath sent him to reproach the living God."

Micah 5:13 — "Thy graven images also will I cut off, and thy standing images out of the midst of thee; and thou shalt no more worship the work of thine hands."

Genesis 14:20 — "And blessed be the most high God, which hath delivered thine enemies into thy hand. And he gave him tithes of all."

Psalm 38:3 — "There is no soundness in my flesh because of thine anger; neither is there any rest in my bones because of my sin."

Modern Corruption

The form is obsolete rather than corrupted. What deserves recovering is the absolute possessive itself — the confession that the kingdom, the power, and the glory are God's and not the worshipper's, in an age fluent in speaking of what is mine.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle needing recovery is doxology — the act of handing everything back. The absolute possessive is the grammar of worship: it does not describe God, it surrenders to Him. David's prayer at the gathering for the temple runs on it, and the closing line of the Lord's prayer in the Authorized Version does the same. A reader who has never used the form still needs the act, and the act is harder than it sounds, because it requires naming out loud what one had quietly counted as one's own.

The nearer misuse is idolatry of exactly the kind Micah names. The prophet's sentence is deliberately cruel to the craftsman: the graven images will be cut off, and then thou shalt no more worship the work of thine hands. An idol is always a possession before it is a god; a man makes it, and then bows to what he made, so that the possessive and the worship contradict each other in a single sentence. Modern idols are less often carved than built — a career, a platform, a portfolio — but the grammar of the sin is unchanged, and so is the remedy, which is that God removes what we will not surrender.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew and Greek make no formal distinction answering to thy and thine; the split is an English one, governed by the sound of the following word. Hebrew suffixes -ka and -k, and Greek sou and sos, cover both.

expand to see more

Saxon þin — the uncontracted possessive of þu; thy is the worn-down form of this same word.

Greek sos (G4674) — thine, the possessive adjective used absolutely, as in thine is the kingdom.

Greek sou (G4675) — of thee; covers what English divides between thy and thine.

Hebrew suffix -ka (H859) — thy or thine, attached to the noun; the English choice between the two forms is euphonic only.

The euphonic rule — thine before a vowel or h, thy elsewhere; the same principle that gives English a and an.

Usage

"Of asking God to turn His own faculties toward a trouble: bow down thine ear, and hear (2 Kings 19:16)."

"Of idolatry convicted by the possessive: thou shalt no more worship the work of thine hands (Micah 5:13)."

"Of enemies given over by God rather than conquered by man: which hath delivered thine enemies into thy hand (Genesis 14:20)."
